title: A New High Water Mark Doesnt Always Reflect True Progress
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece distinguishes between high water marks that reflect genuine progress versus those driven by extra effort, luck, or one-time conditions. Leaders must ask whether a team truly improved in capability or merely worked harder. Real progress reshapes expectations because it becomes repeatable through elevated skills; false progress built on grit alone creates burnout. Celebrating the HOW (the decisions and strategies that led to results) motivates teams to work smarter, not harder. When yesterday's stretch goal becomes today's standard, genuine capability improvements drive motivation toward even higher marks.
points: Not all high water marks reflect real progress; teams dependent on extra effort or luck are actually running in place and risk burnout.
Smart leaders ask: Did we get better, or are we just working harder?—and build sustainable improvement only on genuine skill elevation.
When leaders dissect HOW top results were achieved, they uncover the recipe for repeating them and apply positive pressure to work smarter.
Real progress eliminates excuses: once something has been done through elevated skills, it becomes difficult to argue it cant be done again.
Progress is measured not at the peak but by how far the tide has truly risen—sustained capability, not one-time achievement.
quotes: A High Water Mark in performance is the highest level of achievement or standard that has been reached so far. It becomes an instant reference point for what is possible.
Leaders often overlook the fact that not all High Water Marks reflect progress. Teams that depend on extra effort, one-time conditions, or luck to reach a new level are actually running in place.

True progress elevates skills, capabilities, judgment, and learning. A new High Water Mark built on more skillful execution motivates everyone to work more diligently to reach yet another level of excellence.
What got you to the last High Water Mark won't get you to the next one. What new competency will elevate your game?” Archived from Admired Leadership Newsletter on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
